result.title: Preface
result.summary: Santa Barbara County Employees’ Retirement System (SBCERS) issued an RFP for discretionary private equity consultant services on July 27, 2020. Written questions were due August 10, proposals August 21, and tentative interviews were scheduled for October 28. Proposals must include three printed copies and one signed electronic copy, delivered or emailed to Lauren Thompson at SBCERS in Goleta. The RFP covers SBCERS’ background, investment program and private equity portfolio; required services, minimum qualifications and evaluation criteria; and frequently asked questions. It also sets out proposal-submission procedures, the search timeline, intent to respond, communications and quiet-period rules, addenda, handling ambiguities or omissions, proposal preparation and cancellation. Required proposal materials include a transmittal letter, questionnaire and additional documents. Appendices list current managers and provide the quiet-period policy.

result.title: SECTION I: BACKGROUND & NATURE OF SERVICES REQUIRED
result.summary: SBCERS seeks proposals from qualified firms for a discretionary private equity consulting mandate, preferably with public pension experience. Established in 1944, SBCERS manages about $3.1 billion and provides retirement and related benefits to County, court, and contracting-district employees. The section describes its Retirement Board and investment leadership, consultants and custodian, investment policies, and private equity portfolio: about $311 million (9.9% of assets) against a 10% target as of June 2020. Services include reviewing strategy, allocation, cash flows and pacing; annual planning and guideline updates; sourcing and independently diligencing managers and investments; evaluating and negotiating terms; written recommendations and records; education, research, market updates, document review and Board support. Portfolio monitoring includes capital-call and distribution certification, cash-flow and valuation reconciliation, quarterly and annual reporting, manager-data access, and ongoing performance and partnership monitoring. It also specifies proposer qualifications, proposal evaluation criteria, and FAQs on incumbent participation, planned projects, and Board-meeting attendance.

nodes.title: A. Introduction
nodes.summary:
SECTION I: BACKGROUND & NATURE OF SERVICES REQUIRED
A. Introduction
The Santa Barbara County Employees’ Retirement System (SBCERS) is soliciting proposals from qualified professional private equity consulting firms for a discretionary mandate. Consultants should have private equity consulting experience in the institutional, and preferably, public pension fund area.

nodes.title: B. Santa Barbara County Employees’ Retirement System (SBCERS)
nodes.summary: Established in 1944, SBCERS has about $3.1 billion in assets and provides retirement, disability, death, and survivor benefits under California’s County Employees’ Retirement Law. Members include permanent County and court employees and employees of nine contracting districts: four cemetery districts (Carpinteria, Goleta, Oak Hill, Santa Maria), Carpinteria-Summerland Fire Protection, County Mosquito & Vector Management, County Air Pollution Control, Santa Barbara County Association of Governments, and Summerland Sanitary. The nine-member, two-alternate Retirement Board sets plan policy and oversees investments; four members are appointed by the Supervisors, six elected by members (general, safety, and retirees), and the County Treasurer serves ex officio. The CEO oversees the investment division, led by the Assistant CEO. A general consultant advises on allocation, policy, public markets, and trust oversight; two firms consult on private markets, and BNY Mellon is custodian. Investment policies are in Appendix B/on SBCERS’ website. As of June 2020, private equity totaled about $311 million (9.9% versus a 10% target); managers are listed in Appendix I. The discretionary consultant reports to the Board and works with leadership and staff, reviewing strategies, objectives, allocation, cash flows and pacing; preparing annual plans; updating guidelines and selection criteria; and evaluating, negotiating, and conducting due diligence on opportunities, managers, terms, risks, and track records.

nodes.title: SBCERS Investment Program and Private Equity Services
nodes.summary: SBCERS uses a General Investment Consultant for asset allocation, investment policy, public markets, and Trust policy implementation and oversight, plus two discretionary consultants for private markets, including private equity, real estate, natural resources, and infrastructure. The Bank of New York Mellon is the Trust’s custodian. The investment program refers readers to the Private Equity Portfolio Investment Guidelines in Appendix B and the SBCERS website. As of June 30, 2020, private equity holdings were approximately $311 million, or 9.9% of the fund, against a 10% target; current managers are listed in Appendix I. The consultant is to provide discretionary private equity advice and services, report to the Board, and work closely with the Board of Retirement, CEO, Assistant CEO, and investment staff. The text introduces a list of required services.

nodes.title: 1. Full-service discretionary Private Equity services:
nodes.summary: The provider will deliver discretionary private equity advisory and portfolio-management services: review strategy, objectives, allocation, cash flows and pacing; prepare annual plans covering sub-strategies, markets and diversification; and update portfolio and manager-selection guidelines. It will source and assess opportunities, managers, track records, risks and partnership terms, then conduct tailored, independent due diligence covering strategy, organization and team, capabilities, incentives, commitment, offices, documents, performance verification, references, backgrounds, portfolio-company interviews, and negotiation, with complete written records. Written recommendations will summarize the manager, strategy, terms, expected returns, merits, concerns, negotiable provisions and fit for SBCERS. The provider will review business terms and transaction documents, including amendments; deliver educational presentations, market and industry updates, and interim reviews of existing investments; provide a broad domestic and international manager database; and offer ongoing analytical, research, diligence and partnership-agreement support. It will attend Board meetings when requested and perform other services needed for program success.

nodes.title: 2. Private Equity investments portfolio monitoring services:
nodes.summary: The section outlines SBCERS’ private-equity portfolio monitoring services: review and written certification of capital calls and distributions; wire notifications; reconciliation of cash flows, NAVs and portfolio-company data; quarterly portfolio reports and two annual Board reports; access to manager data; ongoing partnership, performance and cash-flow monitoring; reporting on request; and support with partnership reporting provisions and other program needs. It sets minimum proposer qualifications, including relevant firm and staff experience, institutional clients and assets, suitable database access, E&O insurance, California fiduciary status, and fund-document legal support. Proposals will be evaluated on organization, personnel and clients; investment selection and due diligence; strategic and tactical planning; monitoring, performance measurement and reporting; and fees. FAQs explain that SBCERS seeks the firm best suited to future needs, invites incumbent Hamilton Lane to rebid, has no initial strategic projects planned, and requires at least four annual Board-meeting attendances, with typical meeting scheduling noted.

nodes.title: c. Provide wire notifications to Bank of New York Mellon (custody bank), staff and
nodes.summary: The services include notifying the Bank of New York Mellon, staff, and other relevant parties of wires; reconciling Private Equity cash flows, NAVs, and portfolio-company data with the custodian monthly or quarterly as directed by SBCERS, with results delivered within 30 days of completion; and providing quarterly reports covering managers, partnerships, strategies, and the total portfolio, including commitments, contributions, distributions, values, performance, and benchmark comparisons. Two comprehensive monitoring reports are required annually, after calendar- and fiscal-year ends, for presentation to the Retirement Board, covering developments, market value and funding, performance versus benchmarks, diversification, and other relevant matters. Services also include access to a broad domestic and international manager database; ongoing portfolio and partnership monitoring, performance measurement, cash-flow analysis, and reports upon request; negotiating limited-partnership reporting provisions; ad hoc reporting; and other services needed for a successful program.

nodes.title: F. Minimum Qualifications for Proposal
nodes.summary: To qualify for further consideration, as of December 31, 2020, a proposer must: have at least five years providing similar services; assign professionals with at least 10 years’ private-equity investment recommendation experience (three with the firm), five years analyzing and monitoring institutional partnership results, and five years reviewing partnership agreements and related legal documents; maintain or have unrestricted access to a database adequate to analyze many partnerships across structure, size, industry, geography, type, and development stage; provide private-equity investment management services for at least five years and have at least two pension or other major institutional clients with at least $3 billion in combined assets; carry or have applied for E&O insurance by the RFP submission date and maintain it throughout the contract; currently act as, and commit to remain, a fiduciary under California law, including the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937; and provide or retain, at its own expense, counsel to review and negotiate fund documents, including side-letter provisions addressing SBCERS’ status as a California public pension plan.

nodes.title: H. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
nodes.summary: The Board is conducting a genuine search for the private equity consulting firm best suited to SBCERS’ future needs, consistent with best practices and its fiduciary duty. The incumbent is Hamilton Lane, which is invited to rebid. No new strategic projects are planned at the outset, though the Board will consider recommendations from the selected consultant. The consultant must attend at least four Board meetings annually; investment-oriented meetings are generally held on the fourth Wednesday of each month, except in March, November, and December.

result.title: SECTION II: PROCESS FOR SUBMITTING PROPOSAL
result.summary: Proposals are due August 21, 2020, at 5:00 p.m. PST, with required signatures and seven (3) printed copies plus one electronic copy, submitted to Lauren Thompson at SBCERS by mail or email. The schedule includes the July 27 posting, August 10 deadline for questions and intent to respond, and tentative October 28 interviews; SBCERS may amend dates, and failure to state intent does not bar submission. During the quiet period, Trustee contact with candidates is restricted; questions and reports of errors must be emailed in writing by August 10. Proposers must monitor and incorporate addenda. Submissions must be paginated, indexed, signed, and answer Section III questions in order with requested exhibits. SBCERS may seek clarification, permit minor corrections, or reject responses; revisions must arrive by the deadline through the original method. Proposers bear costs; submissions become SBCERS property and are subject to California law and public-records disclosure, with limited, justified confidentiality designations and related indemnity obligations. SBCERS may cancel the RFP, reject proposals, or end negotiations without awarding a contract.

nodes.summary: Proposals are due by 5:00 p.m. PST on August 21, 2020, and must include seven (3) printed copies and one electronic copy, with required signatures in both formats. Submit them to Lauren Thompson at SBCERS, 130 Robin Hill Road, Suite 100, Goleta, CA 93117, or lthompson@sbcers.org. nodes.title: D. Quiet Period, Questions and Communication Regarding the RFP
nodes.summary: During the consultant search, Trustees may not knowingly contact candidates except for official interviews, due diligence, or ongoing work with the current consultant. Questions about the RFP or proposal process must be emailed in writing to Lauren Thompson by August 10, 2020; the full quiet-period policy is in Appendix II. SBCERS may issue written RFP addenda before proposals are due and post them on its website. Proposers must check for and incorporate all addenda, including shortly before the deadline. They must review the RFP and promptly report ambiguities, discrepancies, omissions, or errors in writing; clarifications or changes will be issued by addendum. Proposals must be sequentially paginated, organized, and indexed as: Letter of Transmittal, Questionnaire Response, Fee Proposal, and Additional Documents and Materials. Authorized principals’ or officers’ signatures are required on the transmittal letter and fee proposal.

nodes.title: G. Preparation of the Proposal
nodes.summary: Proposals must be sequentially page-numbered, organized, and indexed as: Letter of Transmittal, Response to Questionnaire, Fee Proposal, and Additional Documents and Materials. Authorized principals’ or officers’ signatures are required on the transmittal letter and fee proposal. Respond to every Section III question in order and include requested Part C materials as exhibits; answers should be clear, specific, and concise, as incomplete or misleading responses may disqualify the proposer. SBCERS may request oral or written clarification but may award without further clarification. Proposers may revise submissions before the deadline, using the original submission method; revisions must arrive by the due date, and intent or work on a revision does not extend it. SBCERS’s failure to object to proposal errors or deviations does not waive RFP requirements. It may allow correction of minor issues, seek clarification, or take other measures serving SBCERS and beneficiaries’ interests. The text also lists financial responsibility and document ownership as a heading without further details.

nodes.title: Proposal Responses, Revisions, and Errors
nodes.summary: Proposers must answer Section III questions and information requests in order, include requested Part C materials as exhibits, and provide clear, concise, specific responses; incomplete or misleading answers may result in rejection. SBCERS may request oral or written clarification but can award without further clarification. Proposers may revise submissions before the deadline using the original submission method; notice or starting a revision does not extend the deadline. SBCERS’s failure to object to proposal errors or omissions does not waive RFP requirements. SBCERS may waive or allow correction of minor issues before final evaluation, seek clarification, or take other measures in its and its beneficiaries’ best interests.

nodes.title: 5. Financial Responsibility and Ownership of Documents
nodes.summary: Proposing firms bear all costs of preparing, submitting, and presenting proposals; proposals and related materials become SBCERS property and may be returned at its option. California law governs the procurement and resulting agreements, and submitting a proposal accepts this condition. Proposals are subject to the California Public Records Act and may be publicly inspected or copied after contract award. Potentially exempt portions must be separately marked “TRADE SECRETS,” “CONFIDENTIAL,” or “PROPRIETARY”; marking an entire proposal does not make it exempt. Firms must have a good-faith basis for such designations and may need to justify them in writing; designations are not conclusive. If SBCERS withholds designated material, or discloses it because disclosure is legally required or court-ordered, the firm must reimburse, indemnify, defend, and hold SBCERS and associated personnel harmless from related claims, losses, costs, and expenses, including legal fees.

nodes.title: Proposal Costs, Governing Law, and Public Records
nodes.summary: Proposers bear all costs of preparing, submitting, and presenting proposals; submissions become SBCERS property and may be returned at its option. nodes.title: H. Cancellation of the RFP
nodes.summary:
H. Cancellation of the RFP
SBCERS reserves the right to cancel this RFP at any time, and to reject any and all proposals submitted in response to this RFP if it is in SBCERS’ best interest. This RFP in no manner obligates SBCERS to the procurement of services until a written contract is entered into, negotiation of which may be terminated at any time by SBCERS. If negotiations fail, SBCERS may accept another submitted proposal, at its option. SBCERS may terminate negotiations at any time prior to the signing of a contract.

result.title: SECTION III: INFORMATION TO BE PROVIDED
result.summary: Section III specifies the proposal information to be provided. Part A requires a signed transmittal letter from an authorized representative, including firm and signer contact details; confirmation of signing authority, a six-month irrevocable offer, staff and resource availability, minimum-qualification compliance, willingness to accept a fiduciary obligation to SBCERS, and acknowledgment of public-record disclosure subject to applicable exemptions. Part B requires a signed introduction and executive summary, requested attachments, answers to all questions, and figures as of December 31, 2019 unless stated otherwise. It addresses minimum qualifications, including experience, data access, institutional clients and assets, insurance, fiduciary services, and legal-document review. Firm questions cover history, staffing, investments, commitments, ownership, structure and changes, revenues, compensation and relationships, conflicts and safeguards, registration, litigation or investigations, and staff biographies. Assigned professionals’ profiles must provide role, location, experience, education, language skills, designations, and lead-consultant client count.

nodes.title: Part A: Letter of Transmittal
nodes.summary: Section III requires a signed Letter of Transmittal or cover letter, forming part of the proposal, from someone authorized to bind the firm. It must provide the proposer’s contact details and signer’s name, title, phone, and email; confirm signing authority, a firm irrevocable six-month offer, availability of staff and resources to deliver all services, and compliance with Section I.F minimum qualifications; state willingness, if selected, to contractually accept a fiduciary obligation to SBCERS; and acknowledge that submitted documents become public records except portions determined exempt under the Act, as described in Section II.G. Part B is a Questionnaire.

nodes.title: Introduction and Executive Summary
nodes.summary: The proposal must include an introduction letter and executive summary, signed by someone authorized to bind the firm; submission represents the firm’s willingness and ability to meet its commitments. Attach requested documents, answer all questions, and use figures as of December 31, 2019 unless otherwise specified. Minimum-qualification questions cover: at least five years providing similar services; assigned professionals’ required experience recommending, analyzing, monitoring, and reviewing private-equity investments and legal documents; access to a sufficiently broad partnership-returns database; at least five years providing private-equity investment-management services and two institutional clients with at least $3 billion in total assets; Errors and Omissions coverage or an application, with coverage maintained during the contract; current and proposed fiduciary service under California law; and willingness to provide or retain counsel at the firm’s expense to review and negotiate fund documents, including side letters reflecting SBCERS’ public-pension status. The organization section requests information about the firm.

nodes.title: Organization Information
nodes.summary: The questionnaire requests firm details, including establishment dates, headquarters, private equity professionals and investments, discretionary account commitments, ownership and employee ownership, organizational structure, anticipated changes, and developments over the past three years. It asks for annual revenue by category for 2015–2019 and, if applicable, the share of the ultimate parent’s income represented by consulting services in those years. For 2019, it requests amounts and sources of non-cash or in-kind compensation, beneficial investment-manager/general-partner relationships, and placement-agent financial relationships. It also asks about potential conflicts, co-investments, investment-manager or fund sponsorship roles, and safeguards for objective advice; investment-adviser registration and Form ADV or an exemption explanation; and relevant litigation or regulatory investigations over five years and their status. Finally, it requests biographies and resumes for lead professionals and other staff assigned to the account.

result.title: APPENDIX II: QUIET PERIOD POLICY
result.summary: The policy authorizes the Board, through the CEO, to begin a quiet period when a provider search reaches specified stages, an incumbent is placed on watch status, or the Board finds temporary communication limits in SBCERS’s interest. The CEO or staff normally reports this at a regular meeting; urgent periods may begin between meetings, with immediate notice to trustees and later Board reporting. During a quiet period, trustees may not discuss SBCERS business with specified providers except at Board or committee meetings, scheduled due diligence, or routine incumbent business. Socializing is prohibited, except at open industry-conference events with other systems’ trustees or staff, without SBCERS business discussion. Trustees must disclose in writing beforehand to the CEO and Board unrelated contacts; if time is short, notify the Chair or Vice-Chair. Communications include in-person, phone, written, text, social media, and email. Periods end upon authorization to negotiate with a successful bidder, termination of the search, or Board/CEO decision. Providers receive the policy and must agree in writing; RFPs must include it. At selection, retention, or material compensation deliberations, trustees disclose relevant contacts from the prior 12 months, excluding routine incumbent business.
